events.title: Lunar eclipse ends the Pannonian mutiny
events.summary: During the mutiny of the three Pannonian legions in September AD 14, a total lunar eclipse on the night of 26/27 September terrified the soldiers, who banged bronze and blew trumpets to help the moon, and Drusus's agents used their fear to break the revolt.
events.detail: Tacitus (Annals 1.28) describes the moon seeming to fade in a clear sky and the men interpreting the gods' anger. Astronomical calculation confirms a total lunar eclipse visible in Pannonia on 27 September AD 14, which fixes the chronology of the mutiny. The ringleaders Percennius and Vibulenus were then executed.
events.locName: summer camp of the Pannonian legions

events.title: Germanicus buries the dead of the Varian disaster
events.summary: In summer AD 15 Germanicus reached the site of Varus's defeat, where Caecina had gone ahead to bridge the marshes, and buried the bones of the three legions six years after the battle, laying the first turf of the tumulus himself.
events.detail: Tacitus's account (Annals 1.61-62) is one of the most vivid passages in Latin historiography: Varus's first camp with its wide circuit, a half-ruined rampart and shallow ditch where the remnants had made a stand, whitening bones in heaps or scattered, skulls nailed to tree trunks, and the altars in nearby groves where tribunes and centurions had been sacrificed. Survivors pointed out where the eagles were taken and where Varus received his first wound. Tiberius disapproved, thinking a general with augural duties should not handle the dead. The Kalkriese excavations found bone pits containing remains of men and mules buried several years after death, consistent with this episode.
events.debate: Identification of the site with Kalkriese is widely but not universally accepted.

events.title: Recovery of the eagles lost with Varus
events.summary: Of the three eagles lost in AD 9, Lucius Stertinius recovered that of the XIX legion from the Bructeri in AD 15, Germanicus's forces took a second from the Marsi in AD 16 after a traitor revealed where it was buried, and Publius Gabinius Secundus took the third from the Chauci in AD 41, earning the cognomen Chaucius.
events.detail: The recoveries were advertised as balancing the disaster: the arch of Germanicus near the temple of Saturn (AD 17) commemorated the standards recovered "with Varus", and Claudius allowed Gabinius his victory name. The legion numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used again, a unique case in the army.

events.title: Tiber flood and the first curators of the riverbed
events.summary: A great flood in AD 15 led Tiberius to appoint a permanent five-man board of senators, the curatores riparum et alvei Tiberis, and the Senate debated diverting tributaries such as the Chiana and Nar; the towns of the upper valley protested and nothing was done.
events.detail: Tacitus reports the delegations of Florentia, Interamna and Reate, who argued that nature had provided rivers with their courses and that the Velinus should not be dammed into the Nar. The scheme was dropped either from religious scruple or local opposition. Boundary stones (cippi) of the curators, beginning in AD 15 under Ateius Capito, line the riverbanks and record the delimitation of the public bank.

events.title: Clemens, the false Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Clemens, a slave of the murdered Agrippa Postumus, sailed to Cosa intending to rescue his master, and on finding him dead impersonated him, gathering a large following in Italy and Gaul in AD 16 until Tiberius had him kidnapped by agents and secretly executed.
events.detail: Tacitus reports that when Tiberius asked "how did you become Agrippa?", Clemens replied "the same way you became Caesar". Tiberius did not investigate the many in his household and the Senate said to have supported him. The episode shows how fragile the succession still was two years after Augustus's death.

events.title: Storm wrecks Germanicus's fleet in the North Sea
events.summary: Returning from the campaign of AD 16 by the Ems, Germanicus's fleet of a thousand ships was scattered by a storm; many ships were lost, horses and baggage thrown overboard, and some vessels driven to Britain, whose rulers sent back the men.
events.detail: Germanicus was cast ashore among the Chauci, reputedly ready to drown himself. Survivors told tales of sea monsters and half-human creatures. Albinovanus Pedo, a cavalry prefect, wrote a poem on the voyage, of which the elder Seneca preserves a fragment. The losses and cost confirmed Tiberius's decision to recall Germanicus and end the campaigns across the Rhine.
events.locName: North Sea off the Ems estuary

events.title: Furius Camillus defeats Tacfarinas
events.summary: In AD 17 the proconsul Marcus Furius Camillus, with a single legion and auxiliaries, defeated Tacfarinas, a deserter from the Roman auxilia who had organised the Musulamii and Moors on Roman lines, and received the triumphal ornaments.
events.detail: Tacitus notes the irony that the first military glory of the family since the great Camillus fell to a man thought unwarlike. Tacfarinas had divided his followers into a regular infantry and cavalry force and light raiding bands. The victory proved temporary: he resumed raiding in 20 and the war dragged on until his death in 24.

battle.significance: First Roman success against Tacfarinas; triumphal ornaments.

events.title: Strabo completes his Geography
events.summary: Strabo of Amaseia, a Greek from a Pontic family loyal to Rome, completed his 17-book Geography, the fullest surviving description of the Augustan world, in the early years of Tiberius (after AD 18 and before c. 23).
events.detail: He mentions the death of Juba II (AD 23/24, or 18 by an alternative date) and the transfer of Cappadocia; the work was probably drafted under Augustus and revised. Strabo had travelled from Armenia to Etruria and from the Black Sea to the borders of Ethiopia with Aelius Gallus. His geography is a political one, written for statesmen: it praises the unifying peace of Roman rule and preserves much from Eratosthenes, Polybius and Posidonius. His lost Historical Sketches continued Polybius.

events.title: Germanicus crowns Artaxias III of Armenia
events.summary: In AD 18 Germanicus crowned Zeno, son of Polemon I of Pontus, as king of Armenia at Artaxata under the name Artaxias, to the acclaim of the Armenian nobles who liked his native habits of hunting and feasting.
events.detail: The appointment ended the Armenian dispute that followed the expulsion of Vonones (AD 16), whom Germanicus moved to Pompeiopolis in Cilicia; Vonones was killed while trying to escape in 19. Artaxias reigned peacefully until his death c. 34, after which Artabanus II installed his son Arsaces and provoked the crisis of 35.

events.title: Rhescuporis murders Cotys of Thrace
events.summary: After the death of Rhoemetalces I (AD 12) Augustus divided Thrace between his brother Rhescuporis and his son Cotys; in 19 Rhescuporis seized Cotys at a banquet and murdered him, was lured to Rome by Pomponius Flaccus, tried before the Senate and exiled to Alexandria, where he was killed.
events.detail: Cotys, a cultivated man praised by Ovid in letters from Tomis, had married Antonia Tryphaena of Pontus. Tiberius divided the kingdom again, giving Rhoemetalces II (son of Rhescuporis) the west and Cotys's children, under a Roman guardian Trebellenus Rufus, the east. The arrangement lasted until the annexation of 46.

events.title: Fall of Maroboduus
events.summary: Weakened by his defeat by Arminius in AD 17, Maroboduus was driven out in 19 by Catualda, a Gothonian noble with Roman encouragement; he crossed into Noricum and lived for eighteen years as a pensioner in Ravenna, dying in 37.
events.detail: Tiberius told the Senate that Maroboduus had been more dangerous than Philip to Athens or Pyrrhus and Antiochus to Rome (Tacitus 2.63). Catualda was soon expelled by the Hermunduri and settled at Forum Iulii. Their followers were settled beyond the Danube between the Marus and the Cusus under the Quadian king Vannius, whose client kingdom lasted until c. 50. Drusus the Younger, sent to Illyricum, earned an ovation for these diplomatic successes.

events.title: Lex Junia Norbana and the Junian Latins
events.summary: The Lex Junia, probably the consular law of Marcus Junius Silanus and Lucius Norbanus Balbus in AD 19, gave slaves freed informally the status of Latini Iuniani: free during life but unable to make a will, so that their property reverted to their former master on death.
events.detail: Gaius (Institutes 1.22, 3.56) explains that such freedmen "live as free men and die as slaves". They could reach full citizenship by several routes, including marrying and producing a year-old child (anniculi probatio) under the Lex Aelia Sentia, or service in the vigiles. The date is disputed: some put the law in 17 BC under Augustus. The status was abolished by Justinian.
events.debate: Date: AD 19 (consuls Silanus and Norbanus) or 25/17 BC.

events.title: Herod Antipas founds Tiberias
events.summary: Around AD 19 the tetrarch Herod Antipas built Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee as his new capital in honour of the emperor, settling it partly by compulsion, because the site lay over tombs and was ritually impure.
events.detail: The city had a stadium, a palace decorated with animal images that was destroyed by rebels in 66, and a council (boule) on the Greek model. It replaced Sepphoris as capital of Galilee. After 70 and especially after the move of the Sanhedrin in the third century, Tiberias became a centre of rabbinic Judaism where the Jerusalem Talmud was compiled.

events.title: Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls at Lugdunum
events.summary: In AD 19 Gaius Julius Rufus, priest of Rome and Augustus at the Altar of the Three Gauls, built the amphitheatre beside the federal sanctuary at Condate, as its dedicatory inscription records.
events.detail: Rufus, a Santonian aristocrat whose family had received citizenship from Caesar, also built the arch at Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes) dedicated to Germanicus, Drusus and Tiberius in 18-19. The amphitheatre, enlarged under Hadrian, was where the Christian martyrs of Lyon, including Blandina, died in 177. Seats reserved for the delegations of individual civitates survive inscribed.

events.title: Apronius decimates a cohort; Helvius wins the civic crown
events.summary: When a cohort fled before Tacfarinas in AD 20, the proconsul Lucius Apronius revived the old punishment of decimation, clubbing every tenth man to death; soon after, a detachment of 500 veterans routed Tacfarinas at Thala, where the common soldier Helvius Rufus won the corona civica.
events.detail: Tacitus says Apronius awarded Helvius the torques and spear himself and Tiberius added the civic crown, regretting that the proconsul had not given it under his own authority. Rufus is known from an inscription at Tibur as Marcus Helvius Rufus Civica, later primus pilus. Decimation was rarely used under the Principate; Galba applied it to the marines in 68.

battle.significance: Revived decimation and the civic crown of Helvius Rufus.

events.title: Senate decrees a ten-day interval before executions
events.summary: After the knight Clutorius Priscus was condemned and executed on the same day in AD 21 for composing a poem anticipating the death of Drusus, Tiberius had the Senate decree that its sentences should not be registered at the treasury, and so executed, for ten days.
events.detail: Tacitus says the measure gave Tiberius time to intervene but that he never softened a sentence. The case, in which Marcus Lepidus argued for exile against the consul designate's proposal of death, illustrates the elastic use of maiestas charges for words and writings under Tiberius. Dio (57.20.4) dates the measure to the same year.

events.title: Junius Blaesus's campaign against Tacfarinas
events.summary: When Tacfarinas demanded land and threatened endless war, Tiberius sent Quintus Junius Blaesus, Sejanus's uncle, who in AD 22-23 broke the revolt into small mobile columns and kept his troops in winter forts, capturing Tacfarinas's brother.
events.detail: Blaesus offered amnesty to all except the leader and divided the theatre into three sectors. Tiberius granted him the triumphal ornaments and allowed his troops to hail him imperator, the last time a commander outside the imperial family received the acclamation. The legion IX Hispana, sent from Pannonia, was recalled in 23; Tacfarinas promptly reappeared and was finally killed by Dolabella in 24.

events.title: Drusus the Younger receives tribunician power
events.summary: In AD 22 Tiberius asked the Senate to give his son Drusus the tribunician power, the "title of the highest rank", marking him unmistakably as heir.
events.detail: Tacitus says Marcus Silanus and Quintus Haterius proposed fawning honours that Tiberius rejected. The grant intensified the rivalry between Drusus and Sejanus, whom Drusus had struck; Drusus died in September 23, reputedly poisoned by Sejanus and Livilla, as Sejanus's divorced wife Apicata revealed in 31.

events.title: Smyrna wins the provincial temple of Tiberius
events.summary: In AD 26 eleven cities of Asia competed before the Senate for the honour of building a temple to Tiberius, Livia and the Senate voted in 23; the Senate chose Smyrna after hearing delegates cite their ancient loyalty, while Tiberius declined a similar request from Hispania Ulterior in 25.
events.detail: Tacitus summarises the claims: Ilium for its Trojan origins, Halicarnassus for its freedom from earthquakes for 1,200 years, Pergamum because it already had the temple of Augustus, Sardis for kinship with the Etruscans. Smyrna pointed to its temple of Roma founded in 195 BC. Tiberius told the Senate that he was mortal and that the best temples were in their memory, rejecting worship in Spain.

events.title: Pilate brings the standards into Jerusalem
events.summary: Soon after his arrival as prefect of Judaea (26), Pontius Pilate sent troops into Jerusalem by night with standards bearing the emperor's image; crowds besieged him at Caesarea for five days and bared their necks to his soldiers rather than accept them, and Pilate withdrew the standards.
events.detail: Josephus presents the incident as the first of several clashes. Earlier prefects had avoided bringing iconic standards into the city. Pilate's title is confirmed by the inscription found in the theatre at Caesarea in 1961, recording a Tiberieum dedicated by "[Pon]tius Pilatus [praef]ectus Iuda[ea]e". Philo, writing c. 41, describes him as inflexible, harsh and venal, but his ten-year tenure (26-36) was the second longest of any governor of Judaea, implying Tiberius found him satisfactory.

events.title: Pilate's aqueduct and the massacre of protesters
events.summary: Pilate used the Temple treasury (the korban) to build an aqueduct to Jerusalem; when crowds protested during one of his visits, he had soldiers in civilian dress mingle with them and beat them with clubs, killing many.
events.detail: Josephus gives the aqueduct's length as 200 or 400 stades; it is usually identified with part of the system bringing water from the Solomon's Pools area south of Bethlehem. The date within his prefecture is unknown. Luke 13.1 mentions "the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices", another unparalleled incident.

events.title: Public ministry of Jesus in Galilee and Judaea
events.summary: After his baptism by John, Jesus of Nazareth preached the coming kingdom of God, mainly in the Galilean villages around Capernaum, gathered twelve disciples and acquired a reputation as healer and exorcist, over a period of one to three years ending with his execution at Jerusalem c. 30 or 33.
events.detail: Luke 3.1 dates John's appearance to the fifteenth year of Tiberius, which most reckon AD 28/29. The Synoptic gospels imply a single year with one Passover, John three Passovers. Jesus's preaching drew on Jewish apocalyptic expectation, and he avoided the Hellenised cities of Sepphoris and Tiberias. Josephus's Testimonium Flavianum (Antiquities 18.63-64) mentions him as a wise man and wonderworker crucified by Pilate; it has been interpolated by Christian copyists but most scholars think a core is authentic. The excavated first-century synagogue at Magdala and the boat from the Sea of Galilee illustrate the setting.
events.locName: Capernaum and the Sea of Galilee
events.debate: Length of the ministry (one or three years) and authenticity of the Testimonium Flavianum.

events.title: Execution of John the Baptist
events.summary: Herod Antipas imprisoned the popular preacher John the Baptist at Machaerus and executed him, probably c. 28-30; Josephus says Antipas feared he would raise a revolt, while the gospels blame John's condemnation of Antipas's marriage to Herodias.
events.detail: John baptised in the Jordan for the forgiveness of sins and preached imminent judgement; Jesus was among those he baptised. The gospels add the story of Salome's dance and the head on a platter (Mark 6.17-29). Josephus reports that when Antipas's army was destroyed by Aretas IV of Nabataea in 36, many Jews saw it as divine punishment for John's death, which is why his account appears in that context. John's followers persisted independently into the 50s (Acts 19.1-7).
events.debate: Date uncertain (c. 28-30); the gospel motive and Josephus's political motive may both be true.

events.title: Fire on the Caelian Hill
events.summary: A fire in AD 27, soon after the Fidenae disaster, burned the Caelian Hill; Tiberius compensated owners, and a statue of him in the house of the senator Junius that survived was hailed as a sign of divine favour, so that the Senate proposed renaming the hill Mons Augustus.
events.detail: Tacitus says people blamed the emperor's absence and the ill-omened year until his generosity changed their mood. Fires recurred on the Aventine and around the Circus in 36, when Tiberius paid out 100 million sesterces and four grandsons-in-law assessed the damage.

events.title: Velleius Paterculus publishes his history
events.summary: In AD 30 Velleius Paterculus, an equestrian officer who had served under Tiberius in Germany and Pannonia, dedicated a two-book summary of Roman history to Marcus Vinicius, consul that year.
events.detail: The second book becomes a detailed eyewitness account of Tiberius's campaigns and an unqualified panegyric of Tiberius and of Sejanus, whom Velleius calls "singularis principalium operum adiutor" a year before his fall. Despite its sycophancy it is the only contemporary narrative of the Illyrian revolt and the Varian disaster, and it contains early literary history, including essays on the clustering of genius in short periods.

events.title: Arrest of Asinius Gallus
events.summary: In AD 30 Gaius Asinius Gallus, son of Asinius Pollio and husband of Tiberius's first wife Vipsania, was condemned in absentia while dining as Tiberius's guest on Capri, and kept in solitary confinement for three years until he starved to death in 33.
events.detail: Gallus had spoken freely in the Senate since 14 and was one of the potential heirs Augustus was said to have named as "capable but unwilling" or "willing but unworthy". Dio (58.3) notes the cruelty of keeping him alive in isolation. His fall was part of the destruction of Agrippina's party that preceded Sejanus's own collapse.

events.title: Valerius Maximus publishes Memorable Deeds and Sayings
events.summary: About AD 31 Valerius Maximus dedicated to Tiberius nine books of Memorable Deeds and Sayings, nearly a thousand moral exempla arranged by theme, Roman and foreign, for use by orators.
events.detail: A passage (9.11.ext.4) denouncing an unnamed would-be parricide who planned to destroy the empire is generally taken as referring to Sejanus, which dates publication soon after October 31. Despised by modern critics for its style, the work was hugely popular in late antiquity and the Middle Ages, survives in many manuscripts and two ancient epitomes, and preserves much lost material, including from Livy.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Bel at Palmyra
events.summary: The great Temple of Bel at Palmyra was dedicated on 6 Nisan (April) AD 32, according to a bilingual dedication, marking the city's rise as the hinge of caravan trade between Roman Syria and the Parthian Euphrates.
events.detail: Palmyra had come within the Roman orbit under Tiberius: a boundary marker set up by the legate Creticus Silanus (AD 11-17) fixes its territory, and a statue of Germanicus's agent Alexandros records his mission during Germanicus's eastern command. The temple combined a Hellenistic peristyle with Semitic-style crenellations and an off-centre entrance. It was demolished by Islamic State in 2015.

events.title: The phoenix reported in Egypt
events.summary: Tacitus records that in the consulship of Paullus Fabius and Lucius Vitellius (AD 34) the phoenix appeared in Egypt after a long interval, prompting learned debate about the length of its cycle (500 or 1,461 years).
events.detail: Tacitus reports Egyptian and Greek opinion that earlier sightings fell under Sesosis, Amasis and Ptolemy III, and expresses doubt whether this bird was genuine. Pliny (10.5) records that a phoenix was exhibited in the Comitium under Claudius in AD 47, which nobody believed. Phoenix coin types later symbolised renewal of the age (saeculum aureum) under Hadrian and Antoninus Pius.

events.title: Conversion of Paul on the road to Damascus
events.summary: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had persecuted the followers of Jesus, experienced a vision of the risen Christ near Damascus around AD 33-36, and became the most important missionary of the early movement.
events.detail: Paul's own account (Galatians 1.13-24) says he went to Arabia (Nabataea) and back to Damascus, visited Jerusalem three years later to meet Cephas (Peter) and James, then worked in Syria and Cilicia for some fourteen years. He escaped Damascus by being let down the wall in a basket when the ethnarch of king Aretas IV tried to seize him (2 Corinthians 11.32-33), which dates the episode before Aretas's death in 40. Acts gives three dramatised versions of the conversion.
events.debate: Pauline chronology is built back from the Gallio inscription (51/52); dates of 31 to 36 have been proposed.

events.title: Martyrdom of Stephen
events.summary: Stephen, a leader of the Greek-speaking ("Hellenist") followers of Jesus in Jerusalem, was stoned after a speech attacking the Temple, around AD 34; Acts presents Saul as approving witness.
events.detail: Acts 6-7 describes the appointment of seven Hellenist deacons to oversee food distribution, Stephen's debates with diaspora synagogues and his trial before the council. The episode marks the first persecution and the scattering of the Hellenists to Samaria, Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, where the name "Christians" was first used. How a lynching could occur under Roman rule, which reserved capital jurisdiction, is debated.
events.debate: Historicity of the speech and date (c. 31-36).

events.title: Tiberius's Armenian and Parthian intervention
events.summary: When Artabanus II put his son Arsaces on the Armenian throne in 35, Tiberius sent the Arsacid hostage Tiridates III to claim Parthia and backed Mithridates, brother of Pharasmanes I of Iberia, for Armenia; Iberian and Alan forces took Artaxata and defeated the Parthians while Lucius Vitellius advanced from Syria.
events.detail: Tiridates was crowned at Ctesiphon in 36 by the Surena, but Artabanus returned with Dahae and Saka forces and recovered the throne. Tacitus (6.31-37, 6.41-44) gives a detailed account of the intrigues and the Iberian victory. The episode was Tiberius's classic use of diplomacy and client rulers instead of legions, and Mithridates held Armenia until Caligula recalled him.

events.title: Fire on the Aventine and around the Circus
events.summary: In AD 36 a fire destroyed the part of the Circus Maximus next to the Aventine and the buildings on the hill; Tiberius paid owners 100 million sesterces, and four men married to his granddaughters assessed claims.
events.detail: Tacitus says the relief was the more welcome because Tiberius built little for himself. The episode is one of a series of great fires in Rome under the early Principate (6, 27, 36, 64) that shaped the vigiles and building regulations.

events.title: Aretas IV destroys the army of Herod Antipas
events.summary: Aretas IV of Nabataea, whose daughter Antipas had divorced to marry Herodias, and who disputed the border district of Gamalitis, destroyed Antipas's army c. 36; Tiberius ordered Vitellius to take Aretas dead or alive, but the campaign was abandoned on news of Tiberius's death.
events.detail: Josephus says Antipas's army was defeated through the treachery of refugees from Philip's tetrarchy who had joined it, and that many Jews saw the defeat as punishment for the killing of John the Baptist. Vitellius marched two legions towards Petra but sent them around Judaea to avoid carrying images through the land, and himself sacrificed at Jerusalem.

battle.significance: Humiliation of Antipas; Roman punitive expedition aborted.

events.title: Pilate removed after the Samaritan massacre
events.summary: In 36 Pilate's cavalry and infantry attacked an armed crowd of Samaritans who had gathered at Tirathana to follow a prophet up Mount Gerizim to find sacred vessels buried by Moses; the Samaritan council complained to Vitellius, legate of Syria, who sent Pilate to Rome to answer to Tiberius.
events.detail: Pilate reached Rome after Tiberius's death (March 37) and disappears from reliable history; later Christian traditions variously made him a suicide, a martyr or a saint (in the Coptic and Ethiopian churches). Vitellius also deposed the High Priest Caiaphas, who had held office since c. 18, remitted market taxes in Jerusalem and restored the High Priest's vestments to Jewish custody.

events.title: Vitellius and Artabanus meet on the Euphrates
events.summary: Lucius Vitellius and Artabanus II met on a bridge over the Euphrates in 36/37, settling the Armenian conflict; Artabanus paid homage to the images of the emperor and sent his son Darius as a hostage to Rome.
events.detail: Josephus dates the meeting to the end of Tiberius's reign and says Herod Antipas hosted a banquet in a pavilion on the bridge and sent the first report to Tiberius ahead of Vitellius, earning his enmity. Suetonius and Dio place it under Caligula. Darius walked in Caligula's procession over the bridge at Baiae in 39.

events.title: Caligula dedicates the Temple of Divus Augustus
events.summary: The temple of the deified Augustus, begun by Tiberius and Livia, was dedicated by Caligula in 37 with two days of races and the slaughter of 400 bears and 400 African beasts.
events.detail: Its site is unknown, though it lay near the Palatine and is shown on Caligula's sestertii as a hexastyle Ionic temple with Caligula sacrificing. Domitian restored it after a fire and added a shrine of Minerva; Antoninus Pius rebuilt it again (his coins show an octastyle temple with statues of Augustus and Livia). A military diploma of AD 90 records that copies of discharge certificates were posted on the wall behind it.
events.locName: between the Palatine and the Forum (site not located)

events.title: Caligula makes Agrippa I a king
events.summary: On his accession in 37 Caligula freed his friend Agrippa, grandson of Herod, imprisoned by Tiberius for wishing aloud for Gaius's succession, gave him a gold chain equal in weight to his iron one and made him king of the former tetrarchy of Philip (Batanaea, Trachonitis, Gaulanitis).
events.detail: Agrippa had spent his youth at Rome with Drusus the Younger and Claudius, and lived on loans from Antonia and Alexander the Alabarch. His arrival in Alexandria in 38 with royal display triggered the anti-Jewish riots there. In 39/40 he received Antipas's tetrarchy, and in 41, for his part in Claudius's accession, Judaea and Samaria, ruling a kingdom almost as large as Herod's until his death in 44.
events.locName: Caesarea Philippi and the tetrarchy of Philip

events.title: Caligula brings the Vatican obelisk to Rome
events.summary: Caligula had an uninscribed 25 m obelisk shipped from the Forum Iulium at Alexandria in a giant ship and set up on the spina of his private circus in the Vatican gardens.
events.detail: The ship, the largest ever seen according to Pliny, carried 120,000 modii of lentils as ballast and was later sunk by Claudius to form the base of the lighthouse at Portus; its hull was found in the 1950s during airport construction at Fiumicino. The obelisk, still bearing its dedication to Divus Augustus and Tiberius, is the only one in Rome never to have fallen; Sixtus V moved it to St Peter's Square in 1586. The circus, completed by Nero, was the traditional site of Peter's martyrdom.
events.locName: Circus of Gaius and Nero, Vatican

events.title: Caligula's popular measures: elections, accounts and tax relief
events.summary: In his first year Caligula published the imperial accounts as Augustus had done, restored elections to the popular assemblies, abolished the 0.5% sales tax in Italy, recalled exiles and allowed the banned works of Cremutius Cordus, Labienus and Cassius Severus to circulate.
events.detail: He also enlarged the equestrian decuries and paid Tiberius's and Livia's legacies in full. The electoral reform failed because candidates would not compete and the assemblies were soon abandoned again. By 39 Caligula had exhausted Tiberius's reserve (reputedly 2.7 billion sesterces), reintroduced maiestas trials and imposed new taxes on lawsuits, porters and prostitutes, collected through posted notices in tiny letters.

events.title: Caligula's reshuffle of eastern client kingdoms
events.summary: In 38 Caligula restored Commagene, a province since 17, to Antiochus IV with a hundred million sesterces of back revenue, gave Pontus to Polemon II, Lesser Armenia to Cotys and part of Thrace to Rhoemetalces III, the sons of Antonia Tryphaena who had been raised with him.
events.detail: Dio and Suetonius present the grants as the extravagance of a young emperor surrounded by eastern princes, but the policy of ruling marginal regions through client dynasts was Augustan. Caligula later deposed Antiochus and summoned Mithridates of Armenia to Rome, which let Parthia regain influence there.

events.title: Exile of Herod Antipas
events.summary: Urged by Herodias to seek the royal title granted to her brother Agrippa, Antipas sailed to Caligula in 39, but Agrippa's letters accused him of conspiring with Sejanus and Artabanus and of storing arms for 70,000 men; Caligula exiled him to Gaul and gave his tetrarchy to Agrippa.
events.detail: Josephus places the exile at Lugdunum, apparently Lugdunum Convenarum (Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges) in the Pyrenees (War 2.183 says Spain). Herodias refused Caligula's offer to keep her property and followed her husband. Antipas had ruled Galilee and Peraea for 43 years.

events.title: Philo leads the Alexandrian Jewish embassy to Caligula
events.summary: After the riots of 38 the Jews of Alexandria sent five envoys led by the philosopher Philo to Caligula, while the Greeks sent Apion and Isidorus; the emperor received them in 40 while inspecting the Esquiline gardens, mocked them for not eating pork and dismissed them as "unfortunate rather than wicked" for not believing him a god.
events.detail: Philo's Embassy to Gaius, written after Caligula's death, is a unique first-hand account of an imperial audience, and his Against Flaccus describes the pogrom and the downfall of the prefect Avillius Flaccus. During the embassy the envoys learned of the order to place Caligula's statue in the Temple. The dispute over Jewish civic status in Alexandria was settled only by Claudius's letter of 41.
events.locName: Rome and Puteoli; audience in the Gardens of Maecenas and Lamia

events.title: Caligula's bridge of boats from Baiae to Puteoli
events.summary: In 39 Caligula built a 3.6-mile pontoon bridge of merchant ships across the bay from Baiae to the mole of Puteoli, paved like the Appian Way, and rode across it in Alexander's breastplate on two successive days.
events.detail: Suetonius gives three explanations: to outdo Xerxes' Hellespont bridge, to frighten the Germans and Britons, or to refute Thrasyllus's prophecy that Gaius had no more chance of becoming emperor than of riding across the bay of Baiae. The requisition of grain ships was later blamed for a food shortage in Rome. The Parthian hostage Darius rode in the procession.

events.title: Caligula separates the African legion from the proconsul
events.summary: In 39 Caligula, distrusting the proconsul of Africa Lucius Calpurnius Piso, gave command of the legion III Augusta to an imperial legate, ending the last case of a senatorial proconsul commanding a legion.
events.detail: Tacitus (Histories 4.48) says the result was rivalry between proconsul and legate over the frontier; the legate became de facto governor of Numidia, which was formally separated as a province only under Septimius Severus. The legion's base moved from Ammaedara to Theveste and, under Trajan or Hadrian, to Lambaesis.

events.title: Caligula's ships on Lake Nemi
events.summary: Caligula had two enormous ships, about 70 and 73 m long, built on the small volcanic lake of Nemi beside the sanctuary of Diana, floating palaces with marble floors, bronze fittings, lead pipes and possibly a shrine.
events.detail: Dated by lead pipes stamped C CAESARIS AVG GERMANICI, the hulls were recovered by draining the lake in 1928-1932 and revealed ball-bearing rotating platforms, bilge pumps and anchors of advanced design. They were burned in 1944 when the museum built to house them was hit during fighting between German and Allied forces; only bronze fittings and models survive. Suetonius describes similar pleasure galleys with baths and vineyards.
